outputs.L1:
**Editor's note:** Carly Fiorina is chief executive of Carly Fiorina Enterprises and former chief executive of HP. She served as an adviser to Sen. John McCain's presidential campaign last year. Fiorina argues that public outrage over Wall Street pay is justified, but that compensation should not be dictated by government mandate.

(CNN) -- Americans are rightly outraged by excessive CEO pay and perks—an outrage made all the more justified when American taxpayers are footing the bill. Our capitalist system functions best when transparency and accountability are firmly in place. On Wall Street, we have seen far too little of either.

Given this climate, it is no surprise that the president and Congress are now moving to address taxpayer anger and restore, in President Obama's words, some measure of "common sense" to executive compensation. The proposed remedy caps top executive pay at $500,000 for institutions that have received bailout funds.

I don't believe this is the right answer, though I understand the impulse behind it. For one, the cap is arbitrary—why $500,000 rather than $400,000 or $600,000? It is also incomplete, applying only to institutions receiving future government assistance. Most importantly, it does nothing to strengthen our economy when government, rather than the market, determines the value of a given position. In America, that determination has always been the province of markets—not bureaucrats.

So what is the answer?

To strengthen transparency, every aspect of CEO pay and perks should be disclosed fully and regularly. This includes private jets, company cars, club memberships, bonuses, stock options, retirement benefits, and salary—in short, anything a reasonable person would consider part of a CEO's total compensation package.

*See Fiorina discuss executive pay, including her own »*

To strengthen accountability, shareholders should vote annually on all aspects of CEO compensation. Ultimately, it is a company's owners who must judge whether a CEO's rewards are commensurate with performance. And because American taxpayers are now partial owners in many of these companies, the government should have a vote as well—in some cases, a substantial one.

Additionally, "clawback provisions"—which require CEOs to return compensation to shareholders when promised results fail to materialize—should become standard practice.

Finally, when a company turns to Washington for taxpayer assistance, it is effectively acknowledging that serious mistakes were made and major bets went wrong. In such cases, CEOs should be prepared to offer their resignations, along with those of their boards. Accepting a bailout must come with accountability for both leadership and governance.

We must not weaken our economy in the process of trying to repair it. These are undeniably difficult times—President Obama himself has described our situation as a "crisis" bordering on "catastrophe." Times like these demand action. But the key is to pursue measures that offer short-term relief while remaining sound over the medium and long term.

Too often, our political leaders respond to crisis and public anger by overreaching—creating new and unforeseen problems that only become apparent with time. In this country, the opportunity to be rewarded for prudent risk-taking is fundamental to our economic vitality and strength. Let us not lose sight of that principle amid our justified outrage over Wall Street's greed and excess.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Carly Fiorina.*

Naturally, both the White House and lawmakers are now scrambling to address this public fury and, in President Obama's words, bring back "common sense" to how executives are paid. Their proposed fix would cap compensation at $500,000 for firms that accepted bailout funds.

Perhaps most importantly, having bureaucrats determine the value of a position doesn't benefit our economy. In America, that determination has always belonged to the marketplace.

So what should be done instead? Genuine transparency requires that every element of executive compensation—private jets, company vehicles, country club dues, bonuses, equity awards, pensions, and base pay—be disclosed regularly and comprehensively. Accountability, meanwhile, means giving shareholders a binding annual vote on executive pay packages. After all, it's the company's owners who are best positioned to judge whether an executive's rewards match their actual performance. Beyond this, "clawback" mechanisms—which allow companies to reclaim compensation from executives who fail to deliver promised outcomes—ought to become standard practice across the industry.

Lastly, any company approaching Washington for taxpayer assistance is essentially confessing to serious errors and failed strategic gambles. Under these circumstances, executives and board members should be ready to step down. Accepting a bailout should come with real consequences for leadership.

We shouldn't undermine our economic system in the process of repairing it. Times are undeniably tough—President Obama himself has called our situation both a "crisis" and a potential "catastrophe." # The Case for Transparency Over Government Caps: Carly Fiorina's Perspective on Executive Compensation

In the wake of the financial crisis and subsequent government bailouts, few issues have generated as much public anger as the question of executive compensation. Carly Fiorina, the former CEO of Hewlett-Packard, has weighed in on this contentious debate with a perspective that acknowledges the legitimacy of public frustration while offering an alternative to heavy-handed government intervention.

## Justified Public Outrage

Fiorina begins by validating the anger many Americans feel toward excessive CEO pay packages and lavish perks, particularly at financial institutions that have received taxpayer-funded bailouts. When ordinary citizens are asked to shoulder the burden of rescuing failing companies, only to see those same companies' executives continue to enjoy extravagant compensation, the sense of unfairness is not merely understandable—it is entirely justified. This outrage, in her view, reflects a legitimate concern about accountability in a system where private gains have been effectively subsidized by public funds.

## Capitalism's Foundation: Transparency and Accountability

At the heart of Fiorina's argument is a fundamental belief about how capitalism should function. She contends that free markets operate most effectively and fairly when transparency and accountability are built into the system. Unfortunately, she argues, these two critical elements have been notably absent from Wall Street's culture in recent years. The lack of clear visibility into how compensation decisions are made, combined with insufficient mechanisms holding executives answerable to shareholders and the public, has contributed significantly to the current crisis of confidence in corporate America.

## Critiquing the Government's Pay Cap Proposal

Despite her concerns about executive excess, Fiorina does not support the government's proposed solution of imposing a $500,000 salary cap on executives at bailout-recipient companies. She characterizes this approach as fundamentally flawed for several reasons. First, she views the cap as arbitrary—an essentially random figure that fails to account for the complexities of different roles, industries, and circumstances. Second, she considers it incomplete, as it fails to address the broader compensation structure, including bonuses and other benefits that can circumvent the intended restrictions. Most fundamentally, Fiorina argues that determining appropriate compensation levels is simply not an appropriate function of government. Instead, she maintains that markets—not bureaucrats—are best equipped to determine the true value of executive talent and leadership.

## A Market-Based Solution: Full Disclosure

Rather than government-imposed caps, Fiorina proposes a market-oriented alternative centered on comprehensive transparency. She advocates for the full and regular disclosure of all forms of executive compensation, not just base salaries. This would include bonuses, stock options, and perquisites that often escape public scrutiny—such as private airplane usage, country club memberships, and other executive benefits. By bringing these compensation elements into the light through regular, mandatory reporting, Fiorina believes that market forces and public accountability can naturally constrain excessive pay practices without the need for arbitrary government limits.

## Empowering Shareholders and Taxpayers

Complementing her disclosure proposal, Fiorina calls for annual shareholder votes on CEO compensation packages. This mechanism would give company owners direct input into executive pay decisions on a regular basis, creating a built-in accountability check. Crucially, she extends this logic to taxpayers themselves. Since government bailouts have effectively made taxpayers partial owners of these rescued companies, she argues that they too should have some form of voting stake in compensation decisions. This proposal represents an attempt to reconcile the public's legitimate ownership interest—created by their financial support of these institutions—with a market-based approach to governance, rather than resorting to direct government control over pay levels.

## Conclusion

Fiorina's position attempts to thread a difficult needle: acknowledging legitimate public anger over executive excess while resisting government overreach into private compensation decisions. Her proposed solution—rooted in transparency, disclosure, and shareholder democracy—reflects a broader philosophical commitment to market-based accountability mechanisms over regulatory mandates, even as she recognizes that the current system has failed to deliver the transparency and accountability that effective capitalism requires.

# On CEO Pay and Government Intervention

Carly Fiorina has weighed in on the contentious debate over executive compensation, offering a nuanced perspective that acknowledges public anger while questioning the government's proposed solution. She begins by validating the widespread frustration many Americans feel when they see CEOs of struggling companies—particularly those that have accepted taxpayer-funded bailouts—continuing to draw enormous salaries, bonuses, and benefits packages. This outrage, she contends, is not merely populist sentiment but a legitimate response to a genuine problem: when public funds are used to rescue failing institutions, taxpayers have a reasonable expectation that executive compensation should reflect the company's actual performance and circumstances, not business as usual.

However, Fiorina draws a sharp distinction between acknowledging the problem and endorsing the government's proposed remedy. She takes issue with the administration's plan to impose a flat $500,000 salary cap on executives at companies receiving bailout funds, characterizing this approach as fundamentally flawed on multiple levels. First, she argues the cap is arbitrary—there's no clear economic rationale for why $500,000 represents the appropriate threshold rather than some other figure. Second, she points out that the policy is incomplete, potentially leaving loopholes through other forms of compensation like stock options, deferred compensation, or perks that could effectively circumvent the spirit of the cap while technically complying with its letter. Third, and perhaps most fundamentally, Fiorina objects to the underlying principle at work: government officials substituting their own judgment for market mechanisms in determining appropriate executive pay. She views this as government overreach that could have unintended consequences, potentially driving talented executives away from companies that need strong leadership most, or creating perverse incentives that don't actually align with improving company performance.

Rather than accepting this top-down regulatory approach, Fiorina proposes an alternative framework rooted in transparency and shareholder empowerment. Her solution centers on two key mechanisms. The first is comprehensive disclosure—requiring companies to fully reveal all forms of executive compensation, including not just base salary but bonuses, stock options, retirement packages, and various perks like private jet usage, country club memberships, and other benefits that often remain hidden from public scrutiny. This transparency, she argues, would allow market forces and public accountability to naturally check excessive compensation practices.

The second pillar of her proposal is mandatory annual shareholder votes on executive compensation packages, sometimes referred to as "say on pay" provisions. Fiorina emphasizes that this mechanism takes on particular significance in the context of bailout recipients, since taxpayers—through government intervention—have effectively become partial owners or stakeholders in these companies. By instituting regular shareholder votes, she argues, the system would give these taxpayer-stakeholders a genuine, structured voice in compensation decisions, rather than leaving them as passive observers subject to whatever arbitrary rules government officials might impose. This approach, in her view, better honors market principles while still addressing legitimate public concerns about accountability, ultimately trusting stakeholders and market discipline over bureaucratic mandates to produce fair and reasonable outcomes.

# Editor's Note: The Carly Fiorina Story

When examining the trajectory of American business leadership and political ambition, few figures offer as compelling a case study as Carly Fiorina. As an editor reviewing her career, one finds a narrative rich with contrasts—corporate triumph paired with controversy, boardroom authority juxtaposed with political aspiration.

Fiorina rose to prominence as one of the most powerful women in corporate America, becoming CEO of Hewlett-Packard in 1999. Her appointment was historic, making her the first woman to lead a Fortune 20 company. She brought a bold, sometimes polarizing leadership style to HP, most notably championing the contentious merger with Compaq in 2002—a deal that faced fierce opposition from board members and the Hewlett and Packard founding families themselves. The merger ultimately went through, but questions about its long-term value and Fiorina's management approach followed her for years afterward.

Her tenure at HP ended in 2005 when she was forced out by the board amid concerns over the company's performance and her leadership methods. For any editor crafting her story, this moment represents a critical pivot point—the transition from corporate executive to public figure navigating the aftermath of a high-profile exit.

Fiorina's story didn't end in the boardroom. She later ventured into politics, running unsuccessfully for the U.S. Senate in California in 2010, and then launching a campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016. Her business background became both an asset and a liability in these campaigns—supporters pointed to her executive experience as evidence of leadership capability, while critics referenced her HP tenure as a cautionary tale.

What makes Fiorina's narrative particularly valuable for editorial analysis is how it embodies broader themes: the challenges women face in breaking through corporate glass ceilings, the complexities of translating business success into political capital, and the way public perception can shift dramatically depending on which chapter of a career is emphasized.

Any thorough editorial treatment of Fiorina must grapple with these competing narratives—not settling for a simple hero-or-villain framework, but acknowledging the genuine complexity of a career that defies easy categorization.

# Why Capping CEO Pay Won't Fix What's Broken

*By a former technology CEO*

I spent over a decade running a public company, sitting across from board compensation committees, and watching proxy season debates unfold like clockwork every spring. I understand the anger driving calls for government-imposed salary caps on executives. When a CEO makes 300 times the median worker's pay while that worker's real wages have stagnated for decades, something feels deeply wrong. I don't dismiss that instinct—I share it.

But I've also seen up close why a government-mandated cap is the wrong tool for a real problem.

## The Cap Doesn't Address the Disease

Salary caps treat a symptom while ignoring the underlying condition. The real issue isn't that some number on a page is too high—it's that compensation has become disconnected from genuine value creation, and that boards have too often served as rubber stamps rather than rigorous stewards of shareholder capital.

A hard government cap, whether set at a specific dollar figure or a multiple of median worker pay, invites companies to simply restructure how they pay executives rather than how much. We've seen this before. Cap salaries, and compensation committees get creative with stock options, deferred compensation, consulting arrangements, and post-retirement perks that don't show up in the same column. The 1990s tax reform that capped the deductibility of salaries over $1 million famously backfired this way—it accelerated the shift toward stock-based pay, which is a major reason equity compensation exploded in the decades since. Government caps don't eliminate excess; they just make it harder to see.

There's also a harder truth: talent markets are global and mobile. A company that cannot competitively compensate a proven operator will lose that person to a competitor, a private equity-backed rival, or a company overseas. This isn't a defense of any particular pay package—many are absurd—but a recognition that unilateral price controls in a global labor market for executive talent create distortions, not fairness.

## What Actually Works: Sunlight and Shareholder Power

If we want to rein in excess, we need to strengthen the people who already have both the standing and the incentive to do it: shareholders and the boards who answer to them. Two reforms would do more good than any cap.

**First, radical transparency.** Companies should be required to disclose not just the CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio (a rule already in place but often buried in filings few people read), but the specific performance metrics tied to executive bonuses, in plain language, front and center in proxy statements. Too many pay packages are justified by metrics so convoluted that even sophisticated investors struggle to evaluate whether a CEO actually earned the outcome. If a board wants to pay someone $50 million, it should have to explain exactly why in terms a schoolteacher with a 401(k) can understand.

**Second, binding "say on pay" votes.** Right now, shareholder votes on executive compensation are advisory in most cases—boards can and do ignore them. Make them binding. If a majority of shareholders reject a compensation package, it doesn't go through, full stop. This respects the fundamental logic of a public company: it belongs to its owners, and those owners should have real teeth when they believe management is helping itself to more than it has earned.

I'd add a third piece: clawback provisions with actual force. If earnings are later restated, or if performance metrics were manipulated, executives should be required to return compensation tied to those false results—not just for fraud, but for negligence in oversight too.

## Trusting Markets, Distrusting Rubber Stamps

None of this requires a government price-setter deciding what any individual's labor is worth—a power I'm deeply uncomfortable handing to Washington, whatever the sympathetic goal. It requires empowering the people who already have money on the line to exercise real oversight, and forcing enough sunlight into the process that boards can no longer treat compensation committees as a formality.

I watched too many well-intentioned regulations aimed at Silicon Valley or Wall Street get outmaneuvered within a fiscal year, not because companies are uniquely villainous, but because capital finds the path of least resistance. The answer isn't to build a higher wall. It's to give owners a sharper set of tools and make sure they can see clearly enough to use them.

The people best positioned to say "this CEO is overpaid" are not legislators drafting a formula—they're the shareholders whose capital is on the line, armed with real information and a vote that actually counts.

**Editor's Note: Carly Fiorina is the former chairman and CEO of Hewlett-Packard. She served as an economic adviser to Senator John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign. The views expressed in this commentary are solely her own.**

# Government Pay Caps Are the Wrong Answer to a Real Problem

By Carly Fiorina

President Obama's announcement that executives at firms receiving "exceptional assistance" from taxpayers will face a $500,000 compensation cap is, on its surface, an understandable response to genuine public fury. Americans watched banks and auto companies collapse under the weight of reckless decisions, then watched those same institutions come hat-in-hand for taxpayer money, and now watch as some of their executives continue to enjoy lavish pay. The anger is justified. The policy response is not.

Let me be clear about something before I go further: I have spent my career in the private sector, not in government, and I understand executive compensation from the inside. I also understand that when companies fail—as I experienced myself at HP, where difficult decisions about jobs and pay were sometimes necessary and sometimes controversial—the market, boards of directors, and shareholders are the proper mechanisms for accountability. Government fiat is not.

**The Problem With Government-Set Salaries**

There is a certain political logic to capping pay at $500,000. It sounds tough. It sounds like accountability. It polls well, I'm sure. But governing by applause line is precisely how we got into some of this mess in the first place—policies that sounded good but didn't account for how markets actually behave.

Here is the practical problem: the firms receiving this "exceptional assistance" still need to compete for talent capable of unwinding enormously complex balance sheets, navigating toxic assets, and restructuring institutions back to health. If Washington dictates that the executives capable of doing this work cannot be paid what the market demands, we should not be surprised when those executives leave for firms that didn't need bailouts, or for hedge funds, or for opportunities overseas. We will be left with institutions run by whoever remains willing to work for government-approved wages—not necessarily the most capable hands.

This isn't a defense of the excesses that preceded the crisis. Boards of directors were too often captured by the executives they were supposed to oversee. Compensation committees rubber-stamped packages disconnected from performance. Shareholders were too passive. These are real failures of corporate governance, and they deserve real reform—stronger shareholder rights, more independent boards, greater transparency in how pay is determined.

**A Distraction From Harder Questions**

My concern is that a headline-grabbing pay cap allows the administration to appear tough while sidestepping much harder questions: What is the actual plan for these institutions? When and how does government extricate itself from private enterprise? What happens to the "toxic assets" still sitting on bank balance sheets? These are the questions that will determine whether we emerge from this crisis with a functioning financial system or a permanently diminished one.

Pay caps make for a satisfying news cycle. They do not clean up a balance sheet or restore lending. I worry we are treating a symptom while the disease goes unaddressed.

**Accountability, Not Government Control**

There is also a broader principle at stake. Once the government establishes that it can dictate compensation at private companies that accept assistance, we should ask where that logic ends. Is it limited to firms that took TARP funds? What about firms that benefit from other forms of government support—guarantees, Federal Reserve lending facilities, implicit backing? The precedent being set here is not narrow, and this administration, or a future one, may find the temptation to extend it difficult to resist.

I don't say this to defend executives who mismanaged their institutions into the ground and then collected bonuses anyway. Those cases are indefensible, and I understand why Americans are enraged by them. But the answer to bad judgment by boards and compensation committees is better governance—not a permanent expansion of the government's role in setting private wages.

**What Should Happen Instead**

If firms need taxpayer assistance to survive, there should be strings attached—including real, enforceable restrictions on the specific pay practices that rewarded excessive risk-taking, such as bonuses tied to short-term stock performance rather than long-term soundness. That's a legitimate condition of taxpayer support. But a blanket salary cap, applied without regard to a firm's specific circumstances or the market for the talent it needs to recover, is a blunt instrument for a problem that requires precision.

The president is right that the American people deserve better than what they've gotten from some of these institutions. He is wrong that the solution is for Washington to set salaries. The more durable answer lies in the harder work of fixing the incentives, the oversight, and the governance that failed in the first place—not in capping a number and calling it accountability.

---

*Carly Fiorina served as chairman and CEO of Hewlett-Packard from 1999 to 2005 and was named one of Fortune's most powerful women in business for six consecutive years during her tenure. She served as a senior economic adviser to Senator John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign.*

# Let Shareholders, Not Senators, Set Wall Street Pay

The public's anger at Wall Street compensation is not irrational. When executives collect eight-figure bonuses in the same year their firms required taxpayer bailouts, or when pay packages seem disconnected from performance, citizens are right to ask whether something has gone wrong. That anger deserves a serious policy response—but the response should strengthen markets, not replace them with government pay-setting.

## The Case Against Mandates

Proposals to cap executive pay, set mandatory ratios between CEO and worker compensation, or have regulators approve compensation packages sound satisfying. They are also likely to fail, for reasons rooted in basic economics rather than ideology.

Government pay caps have been tried before, including during the 2008 crisis for firms receiving TARP funds. The predictable result was an exodus of talent from constrained firms to competitors, private equity, and hedge funds beyond the cap's reach. Talent didn't disappear—it relocated. Meanwhile, regulators tasked with approving "reasonable" compensation lack the information that markets aggregate naturally: what a particular executive's skills are actually worth in a competitive market for leadership talent.

There's also a subtler danger. Every dollar of executive compensation that flows through a government-approved process becomes a political football, subject to lobbying, favoritism, and the incentives of whichever party holds power. Replacing market signals with bureaucratic judgment doesn't eliminate the problems people are angry about—it just moves the decision-making to a forum with its own distortions, ones we've seen before in other regulated industries.

## What Actually Went Wrong

The real problem with Wall Street pay wasn't that it was too market-driven—it's that in key respects, it wasn't market-driven enough. Compensation committees stocked with the CEO's allies, golden parachutes that insulated executives from the consequences of failure, and bonus structures that rewarded short-term risk-taking while socializing long-term losses: these aren't failures of capitalism. They're failures of governance and accountability that break the link between pay and performance markets are supposed to enforce.

## A Better Path Forward

Three reforms would address the legitimate grievances without abandoning market principles:

**Mandatory clawback provisions.** If a bank's traders generate profits based on risks that later blow up, or if earnings restated years later, executive bonuses should be subject to clawback. Dodd-Frank made a start here, but enforcement has been weak and provisions too narrow. Strengthening clawbacks realigns incentives without capping anyone's potential upside—it simply ensures pay reflects real, durable performance rather than short-term paper gains.

**Genuine shareholder oversight.** "Say on pay" votes exist but are often advisory and toothless. Making them binding, and giving shareholders easier ability to nominate compensation committee members independent of CEO influence, would let the people whose capital is actually at stake exercise real control—not bureaucrats, but owners.

**Radical transparency.** Require detailed, standardized disclosure of how compensation is structured, including deferred pay, risk-adjusted metrics, and peer benchmarking assumptions. Sunlight lets markets, journalists, and shareholders police excess more effectively than any pay czar could.

## Markets Correct Themselves—When They're Allowed To

The financial crisis exposed real governance failures, and those failures deserve real reform. But the solution to insufficiently market-disciplined pay is more market discipline—delivered through owners empowered to hold management accountable, not through Washington setting numbers on a spreadsheet.

Americans are right to be angry. They should direct that anger toward giving shareholders sharper teeth and executives real consequences for failure—not toward a compensation bureaucracy that will prove less accountable, not more.

counterfactuals.output:
# Rebuilding Trust: Executive Pay and the Soul of American Capitalism

*By Carly Fiorina*

As our nation continues to dig out from the wreckage of the 2008-2009 financial crisis, Americans are asking a legitimate question: how did executives at failing institutions continue to collect enormous compensation packages while shareholders, employees, and taxpayers absorbed devastating losses? This is not merely a populist grievance—it strikes at something fundamental about whether our capitalist system still operates on principles of merit and accountability.

I understand the complexities of executive compensation better than most. I have sat in boardrooms, negotiated pay packages, and made decisions about performance metrics. I also understand that capitalism only works when there is a genuine link between risk and reward, between performance and pay. When that link breaks down—when executives are compensated lavishly regardless of outcomes—we don't have capitalism anymore. We have something closer to crony insulation from consequences.

The financial crisis exposed a troubling reality: compensation structures at many institutions rewarded short-term risk-taking without accounting for long-term consequences. Executives were incentivized to pursue strategies that generated impressive quarterly numbers while building catastrophic exposure that would later require taxpayer intervention. This wasn't capitalism failing us; it was a distortion of capitalism that failed everyone, including, ultimately, the institutions and executives themselves.

## The Danger of Overcorrection

That said, I have deep reservations about government mandating specific compensation figures or micromanaging corporate pay structures. Washington bureaucrats setting salary caps or dictating bonus structures represents a solution that could prove more damaging than the disease. We should be wary of solving a crisis of judgment with a crisis of overreach.

The answer isn't for government to become the ultimate arbiter of what any executive is worth. The answer is to ensure that boards of directors—who bear fiduciary responsibility to shareholders—actually do their jobs. Compensation committees became too cozy, too disconnected from performance realities, and too willing to rubber-stamp packages that bore no relationship to results. This is a governance failure as much as a compensation failure.

## A Better Path Forward

Real reform should focus on:

**Transparency and shareholder voice.** Shareholders—the actual owners of these companies—deserve meaningful "say on pay" votes. Not binding government mandates, but real accountability to those whose capital is at risk.

**Clawback provisions.** Executives who receive bonuses based on results that later prove illusory or fraudulent should be required to return that compensation. Performance pay should mean pay for performance that actually materializes, not performance that evaporates in the next fiscal year.

**Deferred compensation tied to long-term outcomes.** Rewarding executives for decisions whose consequences won't be known for years, paid out only after those consequences become clear, would realign incentives toward sustainable success rather than short-term gains.

**Genuine board independence.** Compensation committees stacked with the CEO's allies are not exercising independent judgment. This is a governance reform, not a compensation mandate.

## Accountability Without Abandoning Capitalism

We stand at a crossroads. One path leads to genuine reform—rebuilding the link between risk, performance, and reward that makes capitalism legitimate in the eyes of the public. The other path leads to a permanent expansion of government control over private enterprise, justified by crisis but persisting long after the crisis has passed.

I believe in the transformative power of free enterprise. I have seen it create opportunity, drive innovation, and lift millions out of poverty. But I have also seen how quickly that system loses public legitimacy when it appears rigged—when losses are socialized while gains remain stubbornly privatized regardless of merit.

The answer to this crisis is not the abandonment of capitalism, nor is it capitalism's uncritical defense. It is the restoration of accountability as capitalism's essential ingredient. Executives should be rewarded generously when they create genuine value—and they should bear real consequences when they don't. That principle, more than any specific policy mechanism, will determine whether Americans continue to believe that our economic system rewards merit rather than mere position.

The choice is not between capitalism and regulation. It's between a capitalism that has integrity and one that has lost its way. I choose to fight for the former.

---

*Carly Fiorina is the former CEO of Hewlett-Packard.*
